title: Air India Mandates Drug Testing for All Pilots After Captain Tests Positive for Marijuana
excerpt: India's flagship carrier will screen every pilot for prohibited substances starting August 14, expanding far beyond the previous 10% random testing rule, after a captain on a Phuket-Delhi flight tested positive following a mid-air altitude loss incident.
body:
• Air India has mandated substance testing for all its pilots starting August 14, after a captain on a Phuket-Delhi flight tested positive for marijuana.
  • Flight AI2379, an Airbus A320neo carrying 137 passengers, suddenly lost about 300 feet of altitude during cruise over Odisha on August 4, hospitalizing eight passengers and four crew members.
  • India's civil aviation regulator classified the incident as "serious" and summoned Air India CEO Campbell Wilson for an explanation.
  • The new testing regime replaces the previous rule requiring random screening of just 10% of flight crew per year, with tests conducted at Gurugram and briefing centers after flights.

Air India has ordered mandatory drug screening for every pilot in its fleet, a sweeping expansion of testing protocols triggered by a captain who tested positive for marijuana after his aircraft suddenly lost altitude mid-flight earlier this month.

The Tata Group-owned carrier issued an internal memo directing all pilots — including those at budget subsidiary Air India Express — to undergo substance testing starting August 14, according to Reuters. Tests will be conducted at the airline's Gurugram academy, at briefing centers and offices after flights, and at pilots' home base locations.

The Incident That Forced the Change

On August 4, Air India flight AI2379, an Airbus A320neo (registration VT-EXO), was cruising from Phuket to Delhi when it abruptly dropped approximately 300 feet in altitude over Odisha. The aircraft was carrying 137 passengers, including three infants, and eight crew members.

https://x.com/thodkyaat/status/2088211393204158890

Eight passengers and four cabin crew were hospitalized following the incident. Their conditions were reported as stable, and the aircraft landed safely in Delhi.

Post-flight screening of both pilots for psychoactive substances flagged a result from the pilot-in-command that required confirmatory testing. That confirmatory test came back positive for marijuana, according to Reuters and Indian television reports on August 12.

"We feel it is important to go further."

— Air India internal memo on expanding pilot drug testing

The Directorate General of Civil Aviation immediately removed both crew members from the roster pending investigation and classified the altitude loss as a "serious incident." The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has opened a formal probe.

Regulatory Response and CEO Summons

India's Civil Aviation Ministry summoned Air India CEO Campbell Wilson on August 11 to explain the circumstances of the flight. The ministry's direct involvement underscores the gravity with which regulators are treating the case.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=KgrHqsZc75M

Under existing rules, Indian airlines were required to randomly test at least 10% of their flight crew per year for prohibited substances. Air India's decision to screen all pilots represents a significant escalation — one the airline framed as a voluntary step beyond regulatory minimums.

Captain CS Randhawa, president of the Federation of Indian Pilots, cautioned against drawing premature conclusions before the official investigation report is released. The AAIB investigation will examine whether the positive drug test was a factor in the altitude loss or whether the two were unrelated.

A Test for Tata's Aviation Ambitions

The incident comes at a sensitive moment for Air India. Since Tata Group completed its takeover of the national carrier in 2022, the conglomerate has embarked on an ambitious transformation — ordering hundreds of new aircraft, merging subsidiary airlines, and investing heavily in service upgrades to compete with Gulf carriers and international airlines.

Singapore Airlines, which holds approximately 25% of Air India, has staked its reputation on the airline's turnaround as well. A safety controversy involving substance impairment at the controls threatens to undermine the carefully managed image overhaul.

What This Means for NRI Travelers

Air India remains the primary carrier for the Indian diaspora, operating the bulk of nonstop routes between India and the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom. For millions of NRIs who fly the airline regularly — often on 14-hour transoceanic sectors — the assurance that every pilot has been screened adds a meaningful layer of safety confidence.

The expanded testing program is now in effect, though the timeline for the AAIB investigation and any further regulatory changes remains unclear.
